outputs.L1:
**Editor’s note:** CNN affiliates report on where job seekers are finding work across the country and how those seeking employment are coping with the situation. Job fairs are growing increasingly popular and drawing record attendance.

**(CNN) —** A record number of senior citizens attended a job fair this week in Loveland, Colorado. The annual event, which targeted people age 50 and older, drew its largest crowd ever—about 900 attendees.

Job seeker Nan Cooper said applicants must do more these days than simply walk into a prospective employer’s office with a résumé.

“[Times] have changed radically,” she told Denver’s KMGH. “I’ve spent countless, countless hours on the Internet and filling out applications.”

**iReport.com:** Share your job-hunt story.

Cooper said she had even applied for jobs through the online auction site eBay.

Read the full report on KMGH.

### Northeast: Job week seeks to resolve “disconnect” between employers and job hunters

Employers in the Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, area say they are struggling to fill 22,000 available positions.

Mayor Luke Ravenstahl said this week that the city would increase its participation in a job-placement program, both financially and through city organizations. He made the remarks at the kickoff event for Imagine Career Week, which connects high school students with employers.

A spokesman for one of the groups sponsoring the week’s events said there should not be so many employers with unfilled positions.

“At the same time, we have young people walking around famously saying that they can’t find a job. There’s a big disconnect there someplace,” Paul Leger of the Allegheny Conference told WTAE.

During the career week, students will visit businesses, while prospective employers will visit classrooms.

Read the full report on WTAE.

### Southeast: Wal-Mart to increase its North Carolina workforce by nearly 6 percent

Wal-Mart said Wednesday that it plans to add 3,000 jobs in North Carolina. The retail chain currently employs 51,000 people at 155 locations across the state.

“In a time when many are suffering, we want North Carolinians to know that we are here to stay,” David Cameron, general manager for the Carolinas, told Raleigh’s WRAL.

He did not say where the jobs would be located. North Carolina is one of eight states with unemployment above 10 percent.

Read the report on WRAL.

### Southeast: Military recruiter sees more prospective airmen

Technical Sgt. Greg O’Conner, an Air Force recruiter in Bradenton, Florida, is staying very busy these days.

“With the way the economy is, recruitment is up,” he told Bay News 9. “I get dozens of calls every day and walk-ins from young men and women interested in joining the Air Force.”

One of his recruits was 20-year-old Dakota Slentz, who cannot afford to attend law-enforcement training school. Slentz said the Air Force offers opportunities for great experiences as well as a great salary.

According to statistics provided by the Department of Defense, the Air Force has met its recruiting goals each month of the fiscal year, which began in October.

Read the full report on Bay News 9.

### West: Sacramento project to create thousands of jobs

A building developer in Sacramento, California, says plans to transform rail yards into a residential and commercial district will require thousands of workers over the next 20 years.

Suheil Totah of Thomas Enterprises told KCRA that initial projects, such as road construction, will create jobs for 3,000 people. The company said more than 56,000 people will be needed for the project over the next two decades.

The 244-acre site will be converted into a mix of homes, businesses, entertainment venues and government offices.

Read the report on KCRA.

### Around the nation

Tennessee will use federal stimulus money to hire 12,000 people age 24 and younger, WSMV reports.

A food company is converting a North Carolina textile plant, bringing 172 jobs to the area, WXII reports.

**Editor’s note:** CNN partner stations are examining where employment opportunities are emerging nationwide and how job hunters are responding to current conditions. Career fairs are attracting growing interest, with some drawing unprecedented crowds.

**(CNN) — Colorado:** Roughly 900 people attended an annual employment fair in Loveland this week, setting a new attendance record for the event. The fair was intended for workers age 50 and above.

Applicant Nan Cooper told Denver station KMGH that finding work now requires much more effort than simply taking a résumé to a potential employer. She said the process has changed dramatically and that she has spent countless hours searching online and completing applications. Cooper has even sought work through the internet auction platform eBay.

*iReport.com: Tell us about your experience looking for work.*  
*See KMGH’s complete story.*

**Northeast: Pittsburgh career initiative aims to connect job seekers with employers**

Businesses in the Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, region report difficulty finding workers for 22,000 vacant jobs.

During the launch of Imagine Career Week, Mayor Luke Ravenstahl announced that Pittsburgh would expand its support for a job-placement initiative, both financially and through municipal organizations. The program brings high school students and employers together.

Paul Leger, representing the Allegheny Conference—one of the organizations sponsoring the week—told WTAE that so many positions should not remain unfilled while young people continue to say they cannot obtain employment. He described the situation as a significant mismatch.

Throughout the week, students will tour workplaces, while potential employers will make classroom visits.

*Read WTAE’s full coverage.*

**Southeast: Wal-Mart plans to expand its North Carolina staff by almost 6 percent**

Wal-Mart announced Wednesday that it intends to create 3,000 jobs in North Carolina. The retailer already has 51,000 employees working at 155 sites across the state.

David Cameron, the company’s general manager for the Carolinas, told Raleigh station WRAL that Wal-Mart wanted residents to understand that it remained committed to North Carolina during a period when many people were struggling. He did not identify where the new positions would be based.

North Carolina is among eight states where unemployment exceeds 10 percent.

*View WRAL’s report.*

**Southeast: Economic conditions produce more prospective Air Force recruits**

Technical Sgt. Greg O’Conner, an Air Force recruiter in Bradenton, Florida, has seen a sharp increase in interest. He told Bay News 9 that recruitment has risen because of the economy and that he receives dozens of daily phone calls and visits from young women and men considering Air Force service.

Among those recruits is Dakota Slentz, 20, who cannot pay for law-enforcement training school. Slentz said joining the Air Force would provide valuable experiences along with strong pay.

Department of Defense figures show that the Air Force has achieved its recruitment target during every month of the fiscal year that started in October.

*Read the complete Bay News 9 story.*

**West: Sacramento development expected to generate thousands of positions**

A Sacramento, California, developer says a project that would transform former rail yards into a combined residential and business district will need thousands of employees during the next 20 years.

Suheil Totah of Thomas Enterprises told KCRA that early work, including road construction, would create employment for 3,000 people. According to the company, the overall development will require more than 56,000 workers over two decades.

Plans call for the 244-acre property to include housing, commercial space, entertainment facilities and government offices.

*See KCRA’s report.*

**Elsewhere across the United States**

- Tennessee intends to spend federal stimulus funds to employ 12,000 people age 24 or younger, according to WSMV.
- WXII reports that a food manufacturer is repurposing a North Carolina textile factory, a move expected to create 172 jobs.

At the same time, the job-search process has changed significantly. Despite these efforts, a significant mismatch remains between available workers and open positions. This contrast highlights a broader disconnect between employers’ needs and job seekers’ skills, expectations, or awareness of available opportunities.

Nevertheless, some companies continue to expand their workforces. The large turnout at recruiting events reflects the intense competition for work, but employers’ reports of thousands of unfilled positions also reveal a persistent mismatch between the skills, experience, location, and expectations of applicants and the jobs available.

In Colorado, record numbers of older workers have attended employment events, demonstrating that the search for work extends well beyond recent graduates and younger employees. Many seniors are seeking jobs to supplement retirement income, maintain health benefits, or return to the workforce after financial setbacks. Their presence has prompted career counselors and employers to pay greater attention to the needs of older applicants, including flexible schedules, part-time opportunities, and assistance with online application systems.

The Pittsburgh area illustrates another side of the problem. Employers there report roughly 22,000 open positions, even as many residents continue to struggle to find suitable work. Some openings require technical training, specialized credentials, or experience that applicants do not possess. Other jobs may offer wages, hours, or commuting arrangements that make them impractical for available workers. Workforce-development agencies are responding with training programs, résumé assistance, and partnerships intended to move job seekers more quickly into high-demand fields.

At the same time, major employers continue to announce plans for expansion. Walmart’s proposal to add approximately 3,000 jobs in North Carolina could create opportunities in retail, management, logistics, and related services. Such announcements are welcome in communities affected by unemployment, although the quality, pay, benefits, and permanence of the new positions remain important considerations for applicants.

Together, these developments show a labor market marked by both urgency and contradiction. Large numbers of people need work, while employers say they cannot find enough qualified candidates for existing vacancies. Closing that gap will require more than posting job openings. It will also demand targeted training, accessible transportation and child care, adaptable hiring practices, and clearer communication between businesses, workers, schools, and employment agencies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compile a national news article on how Americans are coping with unemployment, covering record job-fair attendance among seniors, unfilled positions in Pittsburgh, Wal-Mart hiring in North Carolina, increased Air Force recruitment, and a major Sacramento development project.
counterfactuals.output:
# Americans Scramble for Work as Hiring Pockets Defy National Unemployment

*Record turnout at a job fair for older workers contrasts with unfilled positions in Pittsburgh, retail hiring in North Carolina, stronger Air Force recruitment and hopes surrounding a major Sacramento development.*

Americans are responding to unemployment by widening their searches, changing careers and considering jobs they might once have overlooked, as communities across the country confront a labor market marked by both deep anxiety and unexpected opportunities.

The pressure is especially visible among older workers. A job fair aimed at seniors drew record attendance, reflecting how layoffs, shrinking retirement accounts and rising living costs are pushing more older Americans to remain in the workforce or return to it. Many arrived seeking part-time or flexible work, while others were looking for full-time positions after losing jobs late in their careers.

Yet the employment picture is not uniformly bleak. In Pittsburgh, employers continue to report positions they cannot fill, particularly in specialized fields such as health care, technology and skilled trades. The openings highlight a persistent mismatch: jobs may be available, but unemployed workers do not always have the necessary training, credentials or ability to relocate.

Retail is providing another source of work. Wal-Mart has been hiring in North Carolina, attracting applicants looking for steady pay and benefits amid broader layoffs. Such openings can draw intense competition because they are accessible to workers from a wide range of backgrounds, including people moving out of manufacturing, construction and office jobs.

Economic uncertainty is also benefiting military recruiting. The Air Force has seen increased interest as civilian employment options have narrowed. A military career offers regular pay, health coverage, technical training and education benefits—advantages that can become more attractive during a downturn. The rise in applicants may allow recruiters to be more selective, even as families weigh the demands and risks of service.

In Sacramento, attention is focused on a major development project expected to support construction work and, over time, generate additional jobs through new housing, offices, shops and public facilities. Large projects can serve as an important source of confidence, though their employment impact often depends on financing, government approvals and the pace of construction.

Together, these developments show a country adapting unevenly. Some Americans are delaying retirement. Others are retraining, accepting lower pay, commuting farther or turning to the military. Employers in certain sectors are still hiring, but their openings do not necessarily match the locations or skills of those most in need of work.

The result is a labor market defined by contradiction: crowded job fairs alongside unfilled vacancies, widespread layoffs alongside new hiring, and immediate hardship alongside long-term development plans. For unemployed Americans, coping increasingly means flexibility—and searching beyond the industries and career paths they once considered secure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an article titled around where job seekers are finding work during the economic downturn. Mention Loveland’s over-50 job fair, Pittsburgh’s Imagine Career Week, 3,000 new Wal-Mart jobs, rising military recruitment, and thousands of projected rail-yard development jobs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Where Job Seekers Are Finding Work During the Economic Downturn

As layoffs spread and unemployment rises, job seekers are looking beyond traditional office work and turning to sectors that continue to hire. Retail, transportation, the military and large development projects are generating opportunities, while local job fairs are helping workers connect with employers.

In Loveland, an over-50 job fair is focusing on older workers, many of whom are returning to the labor market after a layoff, a loss of retirement income or an extended absence from work. The event gives experienced applicants a chance to meet employers face to face and learn about openings that may suit their skills.

Such events can be particularly valuable for older job seekers, who may face longer searches despite bringing decades of experience. Career counselors are encouraging applicants to update their résumés, emphasize adaptable skills and become comfortable with online application systems.

Pittsburgh is taking a broader approach through Imagine Career Week, a series of events designed to connect job seekers with employers, training programs and career resources. The initiative highlights both immediate openings and paths into industries expected to grow when the economy recovers. Workshops and networking opportunities also give displaced workers guidance on retraining and moving into new fields.

Retail remains another source of employment. Wal-Mart has announced 3,000 new jobs, offering positions at a time when many companies are cutting payrolls. The openings range from entry-level store work to supervisory and specialized roles, providing opportunities for applicants with different levels of experience.

The jobs may be especially attractive to people who need work quickly, although applicants should compare wages, schedules, benefits and advancement opportunities. In a weak labor market, major retailers often receive large numbers of applications for each opening.

Military recruitment is rising as well. With private-sector opportunities narrowing, more people are considering the armed forces for steady pay, benefits, training and educational support. Recruiters are seeing increased interest from applicants who might previously have pursued civilian employment.

Military service, however, is not simply another job. It requires a substantial commitment and can involve relocation, demanding training and deployment. Prospective recruits should carefully review service obligations and speak with family members, veterans and independent advisers before enlisting.

Transportation and logistics could provide longer-term opportunities. Planned rail-yard developments are projected to create thousands of jobs, both during construction and once the facilities begin operating. Potential positions include construction trades, engineering, equipment operation, maintenance, warehousing, freight handling, administration and security.

Not all projected jobs will appear immediately. Large infrastructure projects can be delayed by financing, permitting or changes in demand. Still, job seekers can prepare by pursuing commercial driving credentials, trade certifications, safety training or technical education related to rail and logistics work.

Together, these opportunities show that hiring has not stopped—it has shifted. Older-worker job fairs in Loveland, Pittsburgh’s Imagine Career Week, thousands of new Wal-Mart positions, increased military recruitment and proposed rail-yard projects all point to places where work may still be found.

For job seekers, the best strategy may be to pursue immediate openings while preparing for industries likely to expand over time. That means attending hiring events, applying broadly, updating technical skills and verifying whether promised jobs are available now or remain dependent on future development.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a late-2000s CNN affiliate roundup about the U.S. job market, beginning with an editor’s note and ending with brief “Around the nation” items about youth stimulus jobs in Tennessee and a food company bringing jobs to a former North Carolina textile plant.
counterfactuals.output:
**Editor’s note:** This is an original, period-style news roundup set during the late-2000s recession. It is not a reproduction of a CNN report.

# Job seekers confront a changing U.S. labor market

Across the country, workers are adjusting to a job market reshaped by layoffs, reduced hours and growing competition for every opening.

Local television affiliates report that employment centers are seeing first-time visitors from industries once considered secure. Manufacturing workers are competing with recent college graduates, while former managers are applying for hourly and temporary positions.

In the Midwest, career counselors say applicants are increasingly seeking retraining in health care, information technology and energy-related fields. Community colleges have expanded certification programs, though some students worry that their unemployment benefits will expire before they finish.

Southern states continue to pursue new factories and distribution centers with tax incentives. Economic-development officials say even modest announcements can bring hope to communities that have lost textile, furniture and automotive jobs. But many projects will take months to begin hiring.

On the West Coast, job fairs have drawn long lines for positions in public safety, transportation and customer service. Recruiters advise applicants to tailor résumés to each opening and emphasize skills that can transfer between industries.

Economists caution that hiring typically lags behind other signs of recovery. Companies may first increase workers’ hours or rely on temporary employees before adding permanent staff.

## Around the nation

**Tennessee:** Federal stimulus money is supporting summer employment for young people from lower-income families. Participants are being placed with public agencies, nonprofit groups and private employers to gain work experience and earn a paycheck.

**North Carolina:** A food company plans to bring new jobs to a former textile plant, offering an economic boost to a community hit hard by the long decline of domestic manufacturing. Hiring is expected as the site is renovated for food production and distribution.
